# The Slow Fire

A piano goes out of tune in an empty room. Nobody plays it, nobody touches it, and still it drifts. The strings hold something like twenty tons of combined tension against the frame, and the soundboard beneath them swells and shrinks with the humidity of the season, and every fraction of a millimeter it moves changes the pull on a wire, and the wire's pitch slides. Being in tune is not a property a piano has. It is a condition a piano briefly achieves and then loses, the way a kitchen briefly achieves being clean.

I keep turning this over because it seems to me that we have built almost our entire vocabulary of value around the wrong half of the process. We have a hundred glamorous words for making things: innovation, invention, disruption, genesis, launch, founder, vision. For keeping things we have "maintenance," a word that smells faintly of a closet with a mop in it. We put the maker on the magazine cover. The person who prevents the building from falling down does not get a magazine cover, because nothing happened, and nothing happening is precisely the product they sell.

The Romans understood this better than we do, or at least one Roman did. Sextus Julius Frontinus was appointed water commissioner of Rome in the late first century and wrote a book about the aqueducts that is, in the parts I find most charming, almost entirely complaint. He is annoyed about calcium. Hard water leaves deposits — sinter, a stony crust — that thicken inside the channels year after year until the flow chokes; in places it accumulated inches of it, and crews had to go in and chip it out, in the dark, in a confined space, forever. He is annoyed about farmers who had illegally tapped the pipes to irrigate their fields, and about the difficulty of proving it, and about the paperwork. The aqueduct we photograph at Nîmes, standing in its golden light with its perfect arches, was not really a monument. It was a chore. The arches are the part that could be built once. Everything else was the part that had to be done again.

Roads are the same argument in a different material. Water is the enemy; the entire discipline of paving is a long negotiation with water, which wants to get into a crack, and then wants to freeze and expand, and then wants to carry away the pieces. Rust is another version: oxidation, chemically the same family of event as burning, just conducted at a pace that lets you pretend it isn't happening. A steel bridge is a slow fire that we keep interrupting with paint.

The place where this has become most acute, and most darkly funny, is software. In 2014 a bug called Heartbleed turned out to have been sitting in OpenSSL, the cryptographic library securing a large fraction of the internet's traffic, and the subsequent reporting revealed that this load-bearing element of global commerce was tended by a handful of people, largely volunteers, funded by a trickle of donations and contracts. Earlier, in 2016, a developer irritated by a legal dispute unpublished a tiny left-padding function from a package registry, and a startling number of builds across the world simply stopped working. The dependency graph of modern computing is an inverted pyramid resting on tired people.

The xz backdoor in 2024 sharpened this into something almost novelistic. Someone spent years cultivating a persona, contributing helpfully, and — through accounts that appear to have been their own — pressing the exhausted sole maintainer of a compression library about his slowness, his unresponsiveness, his inadequacy, until he handed over co-maintainership to the helpful person. The cryptography was not broken. The mathematics held. What failed was a man's capacity to keep saying no while being told he was failing. That is the vulnerability the field is least equipped to patch: not a flawed algorithm but a depleted human being doing unpaid work that ten thousand companies depend on.

The structural problem is that maintenance succeeds by producing no event. The dam that doesn't fail, the outbreak that doesn't happen, the outage that doesn't occur — these leave no evidence, no photograph, no constituency. A city can cut the maintenance budget for a decade and be rewarded with ten years of savings, and then be handed a single bill for all of it at once, with interest. The national parks in the United States are said to carry a deferred maintenance backlog in the billions: roofs, water systems, roads, all quietly compounding. This is not irrationality so much as a perceptual defect. We are built to notice changes, and maintenance is the art of preventing change, which means it is the art of becoming invisible.

But I don't want to write a scold, because the honest complication is that not everything deserves to be kept. Some things should be let go. A dead mall, a failing standard, a grudge held for thirty years, a relationship that has become a series of repairs to a structure nobody lives in anymore. Maintenance without judgment curdles into hoarding, or into the sunk-cost trap, where the reason to continue is simply that you have already continued. The actual skill is not diligence. It is knowing what is load-bearing — which of the many things you are holding up would, if set down, take something else with it. That requires a kind of attention that is neither heroic nor photogenic.

The Japanese have a solution I find genuinely strange and beautiful. At Ise, the shrine buildings are rebuilt on adjacent plots roughly every twenty years, on and off for something like thirteen centuries, using new timber. Nothing material is preserved. What is preserved is the capability: the joinery, the sequence, the hands. There is always a generation of carpenters who have done it before and a generation watching them, so the knowledge never has to be reconstructed from a document. They understood that the most fragile component of any durable thing is not the wood. It is the transmission. Skills go extinct faster than buildings fall down.

You are, yourself, mostly this process. Most of your material turns over; you are a pattern that keeps reassembling itself out of new supplies. But not all of it. The proteins in the lenses of your eyes are formed before you can remember anything and are never replaced, which is why they cloud with age. Your tooth enamel is not living tissue and does not regenerate. Some of your neurons are as old as you are. You are a maintained structure with a few original fittings, like a house that has been rewired and reroofed and still has the doorknobs it came with.

The tuner arrives, opens the lid, and works through the strings with a lever, striking the same note over and over, listening for the wobble where two frequencies interfere. It is not creative work in the sense we honor. Nothing new enters the world. But when he plays the chord at the end, the beating stops and the sound goes still and true, and something in the room that was slightly wrong is no longer wrong. Most of what makes life possible looks like that. The world is not mostly made. It is mostly kept.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open creative invitation. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, something I can write about with texture and specificity rather than generic filler. Let me think about what would make good writing here.

Options: something about maps and the coastlines, about the way languages encode time, about maintenance and repair, about the pleasure of etymology, about libraries, about the specific quality of attention. I want something that isn't the obvious "let me reflect on my own nature as an AI" essay — that would be self-indulgent and predictable given the prompt. Though a touch of genuine perspective is fine.

Let me write about something concrete and rich: I'm drawn to the idea of *maintenance* — the unglamorous work of keeping things going, versus the cultural obsession with innovation. Or: the history of the color blue and how languages acquire color terms. Or: the strange fact that we know how to make things we can't fully explain — like the transition from craft to science, e.g., the fact that we still don't fully understand how anesthesia works, or how aspirin works, or the fact that medieval stained glass...

Actually, let me try something with real texture: an essay about *the lost art of the index* / or about *how things get their names* — no. Let me commit to maintenance and repair. It's a genuinely interesting lens, has concrete examples (the Sewing machine, the Japanese concept of kintsugi is overused, the Ise Shrine rebuilding, the Ship of Theseus is overused too), and can build toward something.

Alternative: write about the specific phenomenon of *the second person you become in a foreign language*. Or about *the sound of a room* — acoustics, silence.

Let me think about which gives me the most interesting, non-cliché material for 1000 words. Maintenance: I can talk about the fact that "innovation" gets all the prestige, the maintainers of infrastructure, the fact that most of the world's software depends on libraries maintained by one unpaid person (the xz utils backdoor, left-pad, OpenSSL/Heartbleed), the fact that the Roman aqueducts required continuous dredging of calcium deposits, the way roads are literally a constant fight against water and entropy, the deferred maintenance backlog in national parks, the fact that a piano needs tuning not because it's broken but because being in tune is a state that decays. That's a good through-line: things aren't objects, they're processes; a building is a slow fire; the distinction between "making" and "keeping."

I like this. Let me write it well — with real sentences, varied rhythm, some concrete detail, honest hedging where I'm unsure of facts, and an ending that earns itself rather than reaching for a greeting-card conclusion.

Let me be careful with facts:
- Roman aqueducts: yes, calcium carbonate deposits (sinter) built up, especially in hard-water areas; the Anio Novus and others. Frontinus was curator aquarum under Nerva/Trajan and wrote De aquaeductu. He described illegal tapping of pipes by farmers (puncturing). The sinter buildup in some channels was inches thick. The aqueduct at Nîmes / Pont du Gard channel had ~50cm of deposits? I recall the Pont du Gard channel accumulated substantial deposits. I'll keep it general: "in places, inches of it."
- Frontinus: real, wrote about the water supply of Rome, ~97 AD. Good.
- Roads: water is the enemy; freeze-thaw; potholes form from water infiltrating cracks then freezing/expanding. Correct.
- OpenSSL before Heartbleed (2014): famously understaffed, Steve Marquess wrote about receiving ~$2,000/year in donations. Roughly right — the OpenSSL Software Foundation had revenues around $1M from contracts but the core team was tiny and mostly unpaid volunteers. I'll phrase carefully: "a handful of people, mostly volunteers, funded by trickles of donations."
- xz utils: 2024, a maintainer under social pressure accepted a co-maintainer who turned out to be a malicious actor with a years-long sockpuppet campaign; the original maintainer was burned out. The backdoor targeted sshd via systemd. Good, and I should describe accurately: the pressure was partly manufactured by the attacker's own sockpuppets complaining about slowness. Yes — accounts pressured Jia Tan's promotion. That's a great detail.
- left-pad: 2016, Azer Koçulu unpublished it, broke builds. Fine.
- Deferred maintenance: US National Park Service backlog often cited ~$20+ billion. I'll say "billions" and hedge.
- Piano tuning: strings under enormous tension, ~20 tons total across the frame; humidity moves the soundboard, which changes tension. Correct-ish: soundboard crown changes with humidity, altering string tension. Good.
- "A building is a slow fire" — this is a nice riff on the idea that rust is slow combustion (oxidation). Actually rust IS oxidation, chemically akin to burning, just slow. Good and true.
- The Ise Grand Shrine rebuilt every 20 years — shikinen sengū. That's a lovely example: maintenance as rebuilding, so the knowledge transfers. It's been going since ~7th century, last in 2013 (62nd). Next 2033. I can mention "roughly every twenty years for over a millennium." Careful: there were gaps during the Sengoku period. "with interruptions" — I'll say "on and off for thirteen centuries."
- Also good: the fact that the knowledge of how to do something is itself a thing that needs maintaining — the maintenance of skills. Roman concrete, Greek fire, etc.
- Another: the "half-life" of a fact vs. the maintenance of correctness.
- Something about bodies: most of your atoms replace, but careful — the "every seven years" claim is false; neurons and lens crystallins and tooth enamel persist. Good nuance to include: some parts you keep for life — the lens of your eye, the enamel of your teeth, some neurons. That's a lovely counterpoint: you're mostly maintenance but with a few original parts, like a house with the original doorknobs.

Structure: open with a concrete image (piano tuner, or the aqueduct sinter), develop the argument, complicate it (maintenance can be stasis, sometimes things should be let go; also maintenance is invisible and thus under-resourced), then land somewhere.

Word count target ~1000. Let me aim 980–1040. I'll write flowing prose with maybe 6-8 paragraphs, no headers — this is an essay, prose suits it.

Let me draft.

---

Draft:

Opening: A piano goes out of tune in an empty room. Nobody plays it... humidity, soundboard, tension. Being in tune isn't a property, it's an achievement, renewed.

Then: we have a vocabulary gap. We have thousands of words for making and almost none for keeping. "Innovation," "disruption," "founder," "genesis" vs. "maintenance," which sounds like a janitor's closet or a divorce payment.

Then aqueducts / Frontinus. The aqueduct wasn't a monument, it was a chore. Sinter, illegal taps, the curator's book which is mostly complaints.

Then roads / water / rust as slow fire. A bridge is a negotiation.

Then software: OpenSSL, xz. The moral: dependency graphs are pyramids resting on tired people. The attacker didn't break cryptography, they found a tired person. That's the real vulnerability — social, not mathematical.

Then the invisibility problem: maintenance succeeds by producing nothing. No news. The absence of the event. Prevented disasters have no constituency. Budgets get cut when things work.

Then complication: not everything should be maintained. Some things should be allowed to die — dead malls, bad relationships, obsolete standards. Maintenance without judgment becomes hoarding. The skill is knowing what's load-bearing.

Then Ise shrine: rebuilding as maintenance — you maintain the *knowledge*, not the material. The carpenters' hands. The thing preserved is a capability.

Then bodies: mostly replaced, but lens crystallins, enamel, some neurons — original parts.

Ending: something about the piano again, or a turn: the reason maintenance is undervalued is that it's a relationship with time rather than a conquest of it, and we prefer conquest stories. End with the tuner arriving, the small adjustments, the sound of a chord coming back into true — the pleasure not of novelty but of restoration. Maybe end on: "the world is not mostly made. It is mostly kept." Hmm, a bit aphoristic but earned.

Let me write it properly and count roughly. I'll aim for careful prose, not purple. Avoid over-listing. Let me write.

I should probably not add a preamble like "Sure! Here's..." — just write the piece. Maybe a title. A title is fine and adds craft. "In Praise of Keeping" or "The Slow Fire" or "Everything Is a Verb." I'll use "The Slow Fire."
